title: FlexGanttFX is Open Source
gist: Dirk Lemmerman open-sourced FlexGanttFX, a 15-year-old JavaFX Gantt-chart framework, under AGPL after commercial development, following the same commercial-to-AGPL-open-source pattern used by iText, Elastic, and Grafana as a way to grow usage while deterring SaaS resale without payment.

themes.theme: AGPL as a deliberate commercial open-source strategy

insights.claim: Dirk Lemmerman open-sourced FlexGanttFX, a JavaFX-based resource-scheduling and Gantt-chart framework, after 15 years of commercial development, choosing this move both to widen code availability and to use the AGPL license as a mechanism for addressing project maintenance.
insights.speaker: Erik Costlow
insights.so_what: A mature, previously-commercial UI framework going open source under a network-copyleft license adds a free option to the small pool of high-performance JavaFX charting libraries, relevant to vendors and enterprises doing desktop-based scheduling/visualization tooling.
insights.quote: Lemmerman open sourced the library after 15 years as a way of increasing availability of the code for use while using the AGPL license as a way to address project maintenance.

insights.claim: AGPL's network-use clause requires companies that modify the software and run it as a service over a network to publicly release their modified source, even without redistributing the software itself, which causes many SaaS firms to avoid AGPL-licensed projects entirely.
insights.speaker: Erik Costlow
insights.so_what: This is the core commercial mechanic behind AGPL-licensed open source: it functions as a soft paywall that pushes SaaS vendors toward a paid dual license, a pattern investors should recognize when evaluating open-core business models.
insights.quote: Companies that modify the library must make their source code available to the public, even if they do not redistribute the modified version.

insights.claim: FlexGanttFX's AGPL choice follows a documented pattern among commercially-viable open source projects, including Bruno Lowagie's iText (an original popular PDF library, whose rationale is covered in his book Entreprenerd), Elastic's return to open source, Grafana's 2021 license change, and MongoDB's earlier use of AGPL before migrating away from it in 2018.
insights.speaker: Erik Costlow
insights.so_what: The recurring AGPL-then-sometimes-migrate-away pattern (MongoDB) versus AGPL-and-stay (iText) gives investors a comparison set for gauging how durable an AGPL dual-license strategy is likely to be for a given vendor.
insights.quote: Larger vendors have made similar decisions, such as Elastic’s return to open source and Grafana’s 2021 license change. Other vendors like MongoDB selected AGPL before migrating away in 2018.

insights.claim: FlexGanttFX achieves high-performance chart rendering by mixing Canvas rendering with standard JavaFX nodes, drawing the chart as a single Canvas rather than re-applying effects to hundreds or thousands of individual FX nodes, allowing complex charts to render at acceptable speed.
insights.speaker: Erik Costlow
insights.so_what: A reusable rendering-performance pattern (Canvas-plus-node hybrid) for desktop/JavaFX developers building data-dense visualization tools where per-node rendering does not scale.
insights.quote: This allows the application to render the chart itself as a single Canvas without re-applying the full effects for every element in the chart.

insights.claim: The framework is built on four primitives (rows forming a resource tree, time-bounded activities placed on rows, layers controlling z-order and visibility, and links expressing dependencies) and models time throughout with java.time.Instant, treating time zones, daylight-saving transitions, weekends, and working hours as part of the data model rather than as display settings.
insights.speaker: Erik Costlow
insights.so_what: Modeling calendar complexity (DST, time zones, working hours) as core data rather than presentation logic is a design choice that materially affects correctness for cross-timezone scheduling and resource-planning software, relevant to any team evaluating it for logistics, aviation, or healthcare scheduling use cases the article names.
insights.quote: Time is modeled with java.time.Instant throughout, and the timeline renders at any granularity from milliseconds to decades, with time zones, daylight-saving transitions, weekends, and working hours treated as part of the model.
